questions.question: Given $0<\theta<\dfrac\pi2$, what is the magnitude of the vector $(\cos\theta)\mathbf i+(\sin\theta)\mathbf j+(\tan\theta)\mathbf k$?
questions.answer: $\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta+\tan^2\theta}=\sqrt{1+\tan^2\theta}=\sqrt{\sec^2\theta}=\sec\theta$, since $\sec\theta>0$ in the first quadrant (D).

questions.question: Which is the negation of the following statement? "If snow is falling, then I will not be at the park."
questions.answer: $\neg(P\Rightarrow Q)\equiv P\wedge\neg Q$. Here $Q$ is \"I will not be at the park\", so the negation is \"Snow is falling and I will be at the park\" (C).
options: If snow is falling, then I will be at the park.
If snow is not falling, then I will be at the park.
Snow is falling and I will be at the park.
Snow is not falling and I will be at the park.

questions.question: A particle whose displacement is $x$ moves in simple harmonic motion such that $\ddot x=-4x$. What is $x$ as a function of $t$ if initially $x=3$ and $\dot x=-6\sqrt3$?
questions.answer: $n=2$ and the centre is $x=0$. Try $x=3\cos2t-3\sqrt3\sin2t$: $x(0)=3$ and $\dot x=-6\sin2t-6\sqrt3\cos2t$, so $\dot x(0)=-6\sqrt3$. Both conditions hold (A).

questions.question: The complex number $z$ is shown on the Argand diagram. Which of the following best represents $i\bar z$? (Diagrams A–D are shown below the Argand diagram, in order.)
questions.answer: $z$ is in the first quadrant at an angle of about $20^\circ$. $\bar z$ is at $-20^\circ$ with the same modulus, and multiplying by $i$ rotates it by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise to about $70^\circ$, still on the unit circle. This is diagram A.

questions.question: $P$, $Q$ and $R$ are three collinear points with position vectors $\mathbf p$, $\mathbf q$ and $\mathbf r$ respectively. $Q$ lies between $P$ and $R$ such that $PQ:QR=2:1$. The position vector of $R$ is given by:
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{PR}=\dfrac32\overrightarrow{PQ}$, so $\mathbf r=\mathbf p+\dfrac32(\mathbf q-\mathbf p)=-\dfrac12\mathbf p+\dfrac32\mathbf q$ (C).

questions.question: For which of these statements, for positive integers $x$ and $y$, is the converse necessarily true?
questions.answer: A: $4+6$ is even but 4 and 6 are not odd, so the converse is false. B: $2^2+4^2$ is even, so the converse is false. C: if $xy$ is odd then neither $x$ nor $y$ can be even, so both are odd: the converse is true. D: $3^4$ is odd but $y=4$ is even, so the converse is false (C).
options: If $x$ and $y$ are odd, then $x+y$ is even.
If $x$ and $y$ are odd, then $x^2+y^2$ is even.
If $x$ and $y$ are odd, then $xy$ is odd.
If $x$ and $y$ are odd, then $x^y$ is odd.

questions.question: Which of the following lines passes through $(0,1,-1)$?
questions.answer: A and C have $x=1$ throughout, so they cannot reach $x=0$. B: $\lambda=-1$ gives $(1-1,\,1-0,\,0-1)=(0,1,-1)$. D: $\lambda=-1$ gives $(0,-1,1)$, which is not the point (B).

questions.question: Which of these inequalities is false?
questions.answer: A: $\dfrac1{1+x}<\dfrac1x$ on $[1,2]$. B: $\sin x<1$. C: $e^{-x^2}$ is decreasing, so its values on $[1,2]$ are below those on $[0,1]$. D: on $[0,\pi/4]$, $0\le\tan x\le1$ so $\tan^2x\ge\tan^3x$ and the inequality is reversed, so it is false (D).

questions.question: Which parametric form best describes the curve below?
questions.answer: All options have a unit-circle projection in the $xy$-plane. The curve spirals down towards the plane $z=0$ while circling, so $z$ decays towards 0, not linearly (A), not like $\ln t$ (C, which would be large negative near $t=0$) and not oscillating (D). Only $z=e^{-0.5t}$ decays towards 0 (B).
options: $\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t)\mathbf i+(\sin t)\mathbf j+(t)\mathbf k$
$\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t)\mathbf i+(\sin t)\mathbf j+(e^{-0.5t})\mathbf k$
$\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t)\mathbf i+(\sin t)\mathbf j+(\ln t)\mathbf k$
$\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t)\mathbf i+(\sin t)\mathbf j+(\cos2t)\mathbf k$

questions.question: Let $\omega=e^{\frac{2\pi i}5}$. What is the value of $(1-\omega)(1-\omega^2)(1-\omega^3)(1-\omega^4)$?
questions.answer: $\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3,\omega^4$ are the non-real roots of $z^5=1$, so $z^4+z^3+z^2+z+1=(z-\omega)(z-\omega^2)(z-\omega^3)(z-\omega^4)$. Putting $z=1$: $(1-\omega)(1-\omega^2)(1-\omega^3)(1-\omega^4)=1+1+1+1+1=5$ (D).

questions.question: Use integration by parts to find $\displaystyle\int\ln(x^2+1)\,dx$.
questions.answer: $u=\ln(x^2+1)$, $dv=dx$, $du=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}dx$, $v=x$. $\displaystyle\int\ln(x^2+1)dx=x\ln(x^2+1)-\int\dfrac{2x^2}{x^2+1}dx=x\ln(x^2+1)-2\int\left(1-\dfrac1{x^2+1}\right)dx=x\ln(x^2+1)-2x+2\tan^{-1}x+C$.

questions.question: Use the substitution $u=e^x-1$ to find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{e^{2x}}{(e^x-1)^2}dx$.
questions.answer: $e^x=u+1$ and $du=e^xdx=(u+1)dx$. $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{(u+1)^2}{u^2}\cdot\dfrac1{u+1}du=\int\dfrac{u+1}{u^2}du=\int\left(\dfrac1u+\dfrac1{u^2}\right)du=\ln|u|-\dfrac1u+C=\ln|e^x-1|-\dfrac1{e^x-1}+C$.

questions.question: Use the substitution $t=\tan\dfrac x2$ to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac1{3\cos x-4\sin x+5}dx$.
questions.answer: $\cos x=\dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$, $\sin x=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}$, $dx=\dfrac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$; $x=0\to t=0$ and $x=\dfrac\pi2\to t=1$. The denominator is $\dfrac{3(1-t^2)-8t+5(1+t^2)}{1+t^2}=\dfrac{2t^2-8t+8}{1+t^2}=\dfrac{2(t-2)^2}{1+t^2}$. So $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{1+t^2}{2(t-2)^2}\cdot\dfrac2{1+t^2}dt=\int_0^1(t-2)^{-2}dt=\Big[-\dfrac1{t-2}\Big]_0^1=1-\dfrac12=\dfrac12$.

questions.question: Convert the line $y=3x-5$ to the form $\mathbf r=\mathbf a+\lambda\mathbf b$.
questions.answer: The gradient 3 gives a direction vector $\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix}$, and $(0,-5)$ lies on the line: $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-5\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question: It is known that $5+6i$ is a zero of the polynomial $P(z)=2z^3-19z^2+112z+k$, where $k$ is real. Find the other two zeroes of $P(z)$.
questions.answer: The coefficients are real, so $5-6i$ is also a zero. Sum of zeroes $=\dfrac{19}2$: $(5+6i)+(5-6i)+\alpha=\dfrac{19}2$, so $\alpha=-\dfrac12$. The other zeroes are $5-6i$ and $-\dfrac12$.

questions.question: It is known that $5+6i$ and $5-6i$ and $-\dfrac12$ are the zeroes of $P(z)=2z^3-19z^2+112z+k$, where $k$ is real. Find the value of $k$.
questions.answer: Product of zeroes $=-\dfrac k2$: $(5+6i)(5-6i)\left(-\dfrac12\right)=-\dfrac{61}2=-\dfrac k2$, so $k=61$.

questions.question: Prove that $\sqrt[3]2$ is irrational.
questions.answer: Assume $\sqrt[3]2=\dfrac pq$ with $p,q\in\mathbb Z$ and $\gcd(p,q)=1$. Then $2q^3=p^3$, so $p^3$ is even, hence $p$ is even (contrapositive: odd$^3$ is odd). Let $p=2m$: $2q^3=8m^3$, so $q^3=4m^3$ is even and $q$ is even. But then $p$ and $q$ share the factor 2, contradicting $\gcd(p,q)=1$. So $\sqrt[3]2$ is irrational.

questions.question: Given that $x$ is a real number and $(x+i)^4$ is purely imaginary, find all possible values of $x$ in exact form.
questions.answer: $(x+i)^4=x^4+4x^3i-6x^2-4xi+1=(x^4-6x^2+1)+(4x^3-4x)i$. The real part must be zero: $x^4-6x^2+1=0$, so $x^2=\dfrac{6\pm\sqrt{32}}2=3\pm2\sqrt2=(\sqrt2\pm1)^2$. Hence $x=\pm(\sqrt2+1)$ or $x=\pm(\sqrt2-1)$. (For these, $4x(x^2-1)\ne0$, so the number is non-zero.)

questions.question: Find all the solutions of $z^5=4+4i$, giving your answers in modulus-argument form.
questions.answer: $4+4i=4\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi4$. Let $z=r\operatorname{cis}\theta$: $r^5=4\sqrt2=2^{5/2}$ so $r=\sqrt2$, and $5\theta=\dfrac\pi4+2k\pi$. So $z=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac\pi{20}+\dfrac{2k\pi}5\right)$, $k=0,1,2,3,4$.

questions.question: On an Argand diagram sketch the locus of the point $P$ representing the complex number $z$ such that $|z-(\sqrt3+i)|=1$.
questions.answer: A circle with centre $(\sqrt3,1)$ and radius 1 (it passes through the origin's neighbourhood: the origin is at distance 2 from the centre, so the circle does not contain the origin).

questions.question: For the locus $|z-(\sqrt3+i)|=1$, find the maximum possible values of $|z|$ and $\operatorname{Arg}(z)$.
questions.answer: The centre $\sqrt3+i$ has modulus 2 and argument $\dfrac\pi6$. Maximum $|z|=2+1=3$. The maximum argument occurs at the tangent from the origin: $\sin\alpha=\dfrac12$, so $\alpha=\dfrac\pi6$ and the maximum $\operatorname{Arg}z=\dfrac\pi6+\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac\pi3$.

questions.question: Prove that for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$, $\dfrac{(x-1)^2+(y+2)^2}2\ge x+y$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{(x-1)^2+(y+2)^2}2-x-y=\dfrac{x^2-2x+1+y^2+4y+4-2x-2y}2=\dfrac{x^2-4x+4+y^2+2y+1}2=\dfrac{(x-2)^2+(y+1)^2}2\ge0$, as the sum of two squares is non-negative. Hence the inequality holds.

questions.question: A particle is undergoing simple harmonic motion centred about the origin. Its equation of motion is $\ddot x=-16x$. Show that $v^2=16(a^2-x^2)$, where $a$ is the amplitude.
questions.answer: $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-16x$, so $\dfrac12v^2=-8x^2+C$ and $v^2=-16x^2+C_1$. At the amplitude $x=a$, $v=0$: $C_1=16a^2$. So $v^2=16(a^2-x^2)$.

questions.question: A particle's position at time $t$ seconds is given by $x=\sqrt3\sin4t-\cos4t$. Express $x$ in the form $R\sin(4t-\alpha)$, where $\alpha$ is in radians.
questions.answer: $R\sin(4t-\alpha)=R\sin4t\cos\alpha-R\cos4t\sin\alpha$. So $R\cos\alpha=\sqrt3$ and $R\sin\alpha=1$: $R=\sqrt{3+1}=2$ and $\tan\alpha=\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$, so $\alpha=\dfrac\pi6$. $x=2\sin\left(4t-\dfrac\pi6\right)$.

questions.question: A particle's position at time $t$ seconds is $x=2\sin\left(4t-\dfrac\pi6\right)$. When does the particle first reach its maximum speed after $t=0$?
questions.answer: Maximum speed occurs at the centre of motion, $x=0$: $\sin\left(4t-\dfrac\pi6\right)=0$, so $4t-\dfrac\pi6=0,\pi,\dots$. The first positive solution is $4t=\dfrac\pi6$, so $t=\dfrac\pi{24}$ seconds.

questions.question: If $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$, show that $z-\dfrac1z=2i\sin\theta$ and $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$.
questions.answer: $|z|=1$, so $\dfrac1z=\bar z=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta$ and $z-\dfrac1z=2i\sin\theta$. By de Moivre, $z^n=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$ and $\dfrac1{z^n}=\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta$, so $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$.

questions.question: Using $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$ with $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$, show that $\sin^5\theta=\dfrac1{16}\sin5\theta-\dfrac5{16}\sin3\theta+\dfrac58\sin\theta$.
questions.answer: $\sin^5\theta=\left(\dfrac1{2i}\left(z-\dfrac1z\right)\right)^5=\dfrac1{32i}\left(z^5-5z^3+10z-\dfrac{10}z+\dfrac5{z^3}-\dfrac1{z^5}\right)=\dfrac1{32i}\left[\left(z^5-\dfrac1{z^5}\right)-5\left(z^3-\dfrac1{z^3}\right)+10\left(z-\dfrac1z\right)\right]=\dfrac{2i\sin5\theta-10i\sin3\theta+20i\sin\theta}{32i}=\dfrac1{16}\sin5\theta-\dfrac5{16}\sin3\theta+\dfrac58\sin\theta$.

questions.question:
Let $z=e^{i\theta}$ where $0<\theta<\dfrac\pi2$. On the Argand diagram the point $A$ represents $z$, the point $B$ represents $z^2$ and the point $C$ represents $z+z^2$.

What type of quadrilateral best describes $OACB$?
questions.answer: $OA=|z|=1$, $OB=|z^2|=1$, and $AC=|z^2|=1$, $BC=|z|=1$ (as $C$ is found by vector addition). All four sides are equal, so $OACB$ is a rhombus.

questions.question:
Let $z=e^{i\theta}$ where $0<\theta<\dfrac\pi2$. On the Argand diagram the point $A$ represents $z$, the point $B$ represents $z^2$ and the point $C$ represents $z+z^2$.

Find $\arg(z+z^2)$ in terms of $\theta$.
questions.answer: The diagonal $OC$ of a rhombus bisects the angle $AOB=2\theta-\theta=\theta$, so $\arg(z+z^2)=\theta+\dfrac\theta2=\dfrac{3\theta}2$.

questions.question:
Let $z=e^{i\theta}$ where $0<\theta<\dfrac\pi2$. On the Argand diagram the point $A$ represents $z$, the point $B$ represents $z^2$ and the point $C$ represents $z+z^2$.

Find $|z+z^2|$ in terms of $\theta$.
questions.answer: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$; the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles. In right triangle $OMA$, $\dfrac{OM}{OA}=\cos\dfrac\theta2$ with $OA=1$, so $OM=\cos\dfrac\theta2$ and $|z+z^2|=OC=2\cos\dfrac\theta2$.

questions.question: Prove that $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}$ for positive real numbers $x,y$.
questions.answer: $(\sqrt x-\sqrt y)^2\ge0$, so $x-2\sqrt{xy}+y\ge0$, i.e. $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}$.

questions.question: Using $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}$ for positive $x,y$, prove that for positive real numbers $a,b,c$ and $d$: $a^2+4b^2+4c^2+d^2\ge8\sqrt{abcd}$.
questions.answer: By the result, $a^2+4b^2\ge2\sqrt{4a^2b^2}=4ab$ and $4c^2+d^2\ge2\sqrt{4c^2d^2}=4cd$. Adding, $a^2+4b^2+4c^2+d^2\ge4ab+4cd\ge2\sqrt{16abcd}=8\sqrt{abcd}$.

questions.question: Consider the line $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Let $A$ be the point corresponding to $\lambda=1$ and let $P(6,0,2)$ be a point not on the line. Find the projection of $\overrightarrow{AP}$ onto the line.
questions.answer: $A=(-3,-1,0)$, so $\overrightarrow{AP}=(9,1,2)$. The direction is $\mathbf d=(2,-2,1)$ with $|\mathbf d|^2=9$. $\text{proj}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\mathbf d}{\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf d}\mathbf d=\dfrac{18-2+2}9\mathbf d=2\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-4\\2\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question: Consider the line $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Let $A$ be the point corresponding to $\lambda=1$ and let $P(6,0,2)$ be a point not on the line. The projection of $\overrightarrow{AP}$ onto the line is $\overrightarrow{AX}=(4,-4,2)$, where $X$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$. Hence find the coordinates of the point $P'$, the reflection of $P$ about the line.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{PX}=\overrightarrow{AX}-\overrightarrow{AP}=(4,-4,2)-(9,1,2)=(-5,-5,0)$. $P'$ is the reflection of $P$ in the line, so $\overrightarrow{PP'}=2\overrightarrow{PX}=(-10,-10,0)$ and $\overrightarrow{OP'}=(6,0,2)+(-10,-10,0)=(-4,-10,2)$. So $P'=(-4,-10,2)$.

questions.question: Use de Moivre's theorem to show that $\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$ and $\sin3\theta=3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$.
questions.answer: $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^3=\cos^3\theta+3i\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta-i\sin^3\theta$. By de Moivre the left side is $\cos3\theta+i\sin3\theta$. Equating real parts, $\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$; equating imaginary parts, $\sin3\theta=3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$.

questions.question: Using $\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$ and $\sin3\theta=3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$, deduce that $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{3\tan\theta-\tan^3\theta}{1-3\tan^2\theta}$.
questions.answer: $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta}{\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta}$. Dividing the numerator and denominator by $\cos^3\theta$ gives $\dfrac{3\tan\theta-\tan^3\theta}{1-3\tan^2\theta}$, which equals $\dfrac{\tan^3\theta-3\tan\theta}{3\tan^2\theta-1}$ (multiply top and bottom by $-1$).

questions.question: Given $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{\tan^3\theta-3\tan\theta}{3\tan^2\theta-1}$, by letting $x=\tan\theta$, find the solutions of $x^3-3x^2-3x+1=0$, expressing them in exact trigonometric form.
questions.answer: Put $x=\tan\theta$: $\tan^3\theta-3\tan\theta=3\tan^2\theta-1$, so $\dfrac{\tan^3\theta-3\tan\theta}{3\tan^2\theta-1}=1$, i.e. $\tan3\theta=1$. Then $3\theta=\dfrac\pi4+k\pi$, so $\theta=\dfrac\pi{12},\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{9\pi}{12}$. The solutions are $x=\tan\dfrac\pi{12},\ \tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\ \tan\dfrac{3\pi}4=-1$.

questions.question: The solutions of $x^3-3x^2-3x+1=0$ are $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}$, $\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ and $-1$. Hence show that $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}+\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=4$.
questions.answer: The sum of the roots is $-\dfrac{-3}{1}=3$: $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}+\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}-1=3$, so $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}+\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=4$.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^2\sqrt{8-2x-x^2}\,dx$ using a suitable substitution.
questions.answer: $8-2x-x^2=9-(x+1)^2$. Let $x+1=3\sin\theta$, $dx=3\cos\theta\,d\theta$; $x=-1\to\theta=0$ and $x=2\to\theta=\dfrac\pi2$. $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{9-9\sin^2\theta}\,3\cos\theta\,d\theta=9\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\dfrac92\int_0^{\pi/2}(1+\cos2\theta)d\theta=\dfrac92\left[\theta+\dfrac12\sin2\theta\right]_0^{\pi/2}=\dfrac{9\pi}4$. (This is a quarter of a circle of radius 3.)

questions.question: Prove the following statement for all integers $n\ge3$: \"If $3^n-4$ is a prime, then $n$ is odd.\"
questions.answer: The contrapositive is: if $n$ is even, then $3^n-4$ is not prime. Let $n=2m$, $m\ge2$. Then $3^{2m}-4=(3^m)^2-2^2=(3^m-2)(3^m+2)$. Since $m\ge2$, $3^m-2\ge7>1$ and $3^m+2>1$, so $3^n-4$ has factors other than 1 and itself and is not prime. The contrapositive is true, so the statement is true.

questions.question:
A particle of mass $m$ kilograms is dropped from rest in a medium where the resistance to motion has magnitude $\dfrac1{10}mv^2$ newtons when the velocity of the particle is $v$ m/s. After $t$ seconds, the particle has fallen $x$ metres. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$.

With a diagram, show that the acceleration is $\ddot x=\dfrac1{10}(100-v^2)$.
questions.answer: Taking downwards as positive, the forces are $mg$ down and the resistance $\dfrac1{10}mv^2$ up (a diagram shows these two arrows on the particle). $m\ddot x=mg-\dfrac1{10}mv^2=10m-\dfrac1{10}mv^2$, so $\ddot x=\dfrac1{10}(100-v^2)$.

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ kilograms is dropped from rest in a medium where the resistance to motion has magnitude $\dfrac1{10}mv^2$ newtons when the velocity of the particle is $v$ m/s. After $t$ seconds, the particle has fallen $x$ metres. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$. The acceleration is $\ddot x=\dfrac1{10}(100-v^2)$. The particle hits the ground $\log_e\left(\sqrt5\right)$ seconds after it is dropped. Find its distance fallen in simplest exact form.
questions.answer:
Velocity at the time: $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{100-v^2}{10}$, so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dv}{100-v^2}=\int\dfrac{dt}{10}$. Since $\dfrac1{100-v^2}=\dfrac1{20}\left(\dfrac1{10-v}+\dfrac1{10+v}\right)$, $\dfrac1{20}\ln\left|\dfrac{10+v}{10-v}\right|=\dfrac t{10}+C$. With $v=0$ at $t=0$, $C=0$, so $\ln\dfrac{10+v}{10-v}=2t$ (for $0\le v<10$). At $t=\ln\sqrt5$: $\ln\dfrac{10+v}{10-v}=\ln5$, so $10+v=50-5v$ and $v=\dfrac{20}3$ m/s.

Distance: $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{100-v^2}{10}$, so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{v\,dv}{100-v^2}=\int\dfrac{dx}{10}$, giving $-\dfrac12\ln(100-v^2)=\dfrac x{10}+C$. At $x=0$, $v=0$: $C=-\dfrac12\ln100$. So $x=-5\ln\dfrac{100-v^2}{100}$. At $v=\dfrac{20}3$: $\dfrac{100-\frac{400}9}{100}=\dfrac59$, so $x=-5\ln\dfrac59=5\ln\dfrac95$ metres.

questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{x^n}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}dx$ for integers $n\ge0$. Show that $I_n=\dfrac{\sqrt2-(n-1)I_{n-2}}{n}$ for all integers $n\ge2$.
questions.answer: Write $I_n=\int_0^1x^{n-1}\cdot\dfrac x{\sqrt{1+x^2}}dx$ and integrate by parts with $u=x^{n-1}$, $dv=\dfrac x{\sqrt{1+x^2}}dx$, so $du=(n-1)x^{n-2}dx$ and $v=\sqrt{1+x^2}$. $I_n=\Big[x^{n-1}\sqrt{1+x^2}\Big]_0^1-(n-1)\displaystyle\int_0^1x^{n-2}\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx=\sqrt2-(n-1)\int_0^1\dfrac{x^{n-2}(1+x^2)}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}dx=\sqrt2-(n-1)(I_{n-2}+I_n)$. So $nI_n=\sqrt2-(n-1)I_{n-2}$ and $I_n=\dfrac{\sqrt2-(n-1)I_{n-2}}n$.

questions.question: The diagram shows a rectangular prism in the first octant created from $P(p,q,r)$ with all edges parallel to the axes and with $OA$, $OB$ and $OC$ as face diagonals ($A(p,q,0)$, $B(p,0,r)$, $C(0,q,r)$). It is known that $\angle AOB=\angle AOC=\angle BOC=\dfrac\pi3$. Prove that the rectangular prism is a cube.
questions.answer:
$\cos\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\overrightarrow{OB}}{|OA||OB|}$, so $\dfrac12=\dfrac{p^2}{\sqrt{p^2+q^2}\sqrt{p^2+r^2}}$ (1). Similarly $\dfrac12=\dfrac{q^2}{\sqrt{p^2+q^2}\sqrt{q^2+r^2}}$ (2) and $\dfrac12=\dfrac{r^2}{\sqrt{p^2+r^2}\sqrt{q^2+r^2}}$ (3).

(1)=(2): $p^2\sqrt{q^2+r^2}=q^2\sqrt{p^2+r^2}$. Squaring, $p^4(q^2+r^2)=q^4(p^2+r^2)$, so $p^2q^2(p^2-q^2)+r^2(p^2-q^2)(p^2+q^2)=0$, i.e. $(p^2-q^2)\left[p^2q^2+r^2(p^2+q^2)\right]=0$. The bracket is positive since $p,q,r>0$, so $p^2=q^2$ and $p=q$. Similarly (1)=(3) gives $p=r$. Hence $p=q=r$ and the prism is a cube.

questions.question: Show that for $k\ge0$, $2k+3>2\sqrt{(k+1)(k+2)}$.
questions.answer: Both sides are positive, so compare squares. $(2k+3)^2=4k^2+12k+9$ and $4(k+1)(k+2)=4k^2+12k+8$. Since $4k^2+12k+9>4k^2+12k+8$, $(2k+3)^2>4(k+1)(k+2)$, so $2k+3>2\sqrt{(k+1)(k+2)}$.

questions.question: Using $2k+3>2\sqrt{(k+1)(k+2)}$ for $k\ge0$, show that for $n\ge1$, $1+\dfrac1{\sqrt2}+\dfrac1{\sqrt3}+\dots+\dfrac1{\sqrt n}>2\left(\sqrt{n+1}-1\right)$.
questions.answer:
Base case $n=1$: LHS $=1$ and RHS $=2(\sqrt2-1)\approx0.83$, so LHS $>$ RHS.

Assume $1+\dfrac1{\sqrt2}+\dots+\dfrac1{\sqrt k}>2(\sqrt{k+1}-1)$. Then
$1+\dots+\dfrac1{\sqrt k}+\dfrac1{\sqrt{k+1}}>2\sqrt{k+1}-2+\dfrac1{\sqrt{k+1}}=\dfrac{2(k+1)+1}{\sqrt{k+1}}-2=\dfrac{2k+3}{\sqrt{k+1}}-2>\dfrac{2\sqrt{(k+1)(k+2)}}{\sqrt{k+1}}-2=2\sqrt{k+2}-2=2(\sqrt{k+2}-1)$
(using part (i)). This is the statement for $n=k+1$. By induction it is true for all $n\ge1$.

questions.question: Given that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^N\dfrac1{\sqrt k}>2\left(\sqrt{N+1}-1\right)$, is the statement $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^N\dfrac1{\sqrt k}<10^{10}$ true for all positive integers $N$? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: No. From part (ii), $\sum_{k=1}^N\dfrac1{\sqrt k}>2(\sqrt{N+1}-1)$, which exceeds $10^{10}$ when $\sqrt{N+1}>\dfrac{10^{10}}2+1$, i.e. $N>\left(\dfrac{10^{10}}2+1\right)^2-1$. For such $N$ the sum exceeds $10^{10}$, which is a counterexample, so the statement is false.

questions.question: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be two non-zero complex numbers with $z_1+z_2+1=0$. Show that $|z_1|=|z_2|=1\Rightarrow\dfrac1{z_1}+\dfrac1{z_2}+1=0$.
questions.answer: If $|z|=1$ then $z\bar z=|z|^2=1$, so $\dfrac1z=\bar z$. Then $\dfrac1{z_1}+\dfrac1{z_2}+1=\bar z_1+\bar z_2+1=\overline{z_1+z_2+1}=\bar0=0$.

questions.question: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be two non-zero complex numbers with $z_1+z_2+1=0$. Also show that $\dfrac1{z_1}+\dfrac1{z_2}+1=0\Rightarrow|z_1|=|z_2|=1$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{z_1+z_2}{z_1z_2}=-1$, so $z_1+z_2=-z_1z_2$. Using $z_2=-1-z_1$: $-1=-z_1(-1-z_1)=z_1+z_1^2$, so $z_1^2+z_1+1=0$. Then $z_1^3-1=(z_1-1)(z_1^2+z_1+1)=0$ with $z_1\ne1$, so $z_1$ is a non-real cube root of unity and $|z_1|=1$. Since the equations are symmetric in $z_1$ and $z_2$, $|z_2|=1$ as well.

questions.question: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be two non-zero complex numbers with $z_1+z_2+1=0$. Hence or otherwise show that $|z_1|=|z_2|=1\Rightarrow z_1^2+z_2^2+1=0$.
